[[File:John A. Gladysz.jpg|thumb|John A. Gladysz]]

'''John A. Gladysz''',<ref>{{cite web |title=ORCID Reference Page |url=https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7012-4872 |website=orchid.org |access-date=2 November 2020}}</ref> an [[organometallic chemist]], is a Distinguished Professor<ref>{{cite web |title=University Distinguished Professors |url=http://dof.tamu.edu/Awards-and-Honors/University-Distinguished-Professor |website=Texas A&M University |access-date=26 October 2020}}</ref> and holds the Dow Chair in Chemical Invention at [[Texas A&M University]]. Professor Gladysz is a native of the Kalamazoo, Michigan area.  He obtained his B.S. degree from the University of Michigan (1971)<ref>{{cite web |title=BS Diploma |url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/rgroup/gladysz/documents/udiploma.PDF |website=Gladysz Research Group |access-date=26 October 2020}}</ref> and his Ph.D. degree from Stanford University (1974).<ref>{{cite web |title=Ph.D Diploma |url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/rgroup/gladysz/documents/PhdDiploma.PDF |website=Gladysz Research Group |access-date=26 October 2020}}</ref>  He subsequently held faculty positions at [[UCLA]] (1974-1982) and the [[University of Utah]] (1982-1998). He then accepted the Chair of Organic Chemistry at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg in Germany.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Pferdeschwänze mit Gespür für Temperaturen|url=https://www.presse.uni-erlangen.de/Aktuelles/2001/Forschung_2001/612Perdeschwaenze.html|website=}}</ref>  In 2008, he returned to North America as a distinguished professor and holder of the Dow Chair in Chemical Invention at Texas A&M University.<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Faculty Web Page|url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/faculty/john-gladysz/|website=}}</ref>

== Early life ==
Gladysz was born in Kalamazoo, Michigan, on August 13, 1952, and grew up in the small community of Galesburg<ref>{{cite web |title=Historical Museum |url=http://hsmichigan.org/resources/local-historical-organizations/galesburg-historical-museum/ |website=Galesburg Historical Museum |access-date=22 October 2020}}</ref> between Kalamazoo and Battle Creek.

== Education ==
Gladysz completed four semesters at [[Western Michigan University]]. He then transferred to the [[University of Michigan]], where during his first semester, he took honors organic chemistry from Prof. Daniel Longone. During the next semester, he began a research project involving cyclophanes.<ref>{{cite journal |title=A convenient synthesis of [3.3]paracyclophane |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/jo00436a033 |journal=The Journal of Organic Chemistry |year=1977 |doi=10.1021/jo00436a033 |access-date=22 October 2020|last1=Longone |first1=D. T. |last2=Kusefoglu |first2=S. H. |last3=Gladysz |first3=J. A. |volume=42 |issue=16 |pages=2787–2788 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> He then enrolled in or audited graduate courses and seminars. He continued research with Prof. Longone for two months after graduating (BS Chem) in April 1971,<ref>{{cite web |title=Gladysz University Diploma |url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/rgroup/gladysz/miscellaneouspast.html |website=The Gladysz Research Group}}</ref> and then headed west to Stanford University, where he immediately joined the research group of Prof. [[E. E. van Tamelen]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Eugene van Tamelen Publications |url=https://academictree.org/chemistry/publications.php?pid=52288 |website=academic tree.org |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref>

Prof. van Tamelen had a long-standing interest in nitrogen fixation, and Prof. Gladysz undertook two projects for his Ph.D. dissertation. One was directed at the mode of activation in nitrogenase, and entailed both molybdenum nitrogen complexes and iron/sulfur clusters;<ref>{{cite journal |title=Biological and abiological nitrogen fixation |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00816a074?journalCode=jacsat&quickLinkVolume=96&quickLinkPage=3020&selectedTab=citation&volume=96 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date = May 1974|volume = 96|issue = 9|pages = 3020–3021|doi = 10.1021/ja00816a074|access-date=22 October 2020|last1 = Van Tamelen|first1 = E. E.|last2 = Gladvsz|first2 = J. A.|last3 = Brulet|first3 = C. R.|url-access = subscription}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |title=Nonenzymic nitrogen fixation |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00785a063 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |year=1973 |doi=10.1021/ja00785a063 |pmid=4687688 |access-date=22 October 2020|last1=Van Temelen |first1=E. E. |last2=Gladysz |first2=J. A. |last3=Miller |first3=J. S. |volume=95 |issue=4 |pages=1347–8 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> the other involved organic transformations mediated by titanium(II).<ref>{{cite journal |title=Direct conversion of aldehydes |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00823a065 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=August 1974 |volume=96 |issue=16 |pages=5290–5291 |doi=10.1021/ja00823a065 |access-date=22 October 2020|last1=Van Tamelen |first1=E. E. |last2=Gladysz |first2=J. A. |url-access=subscription }}</ref> These projects introduced him to working with air-sensitive compounds. He was also greatly influenced by a course on organometallic chemistry taught by [[James P. Collman]]. There was an extensive flow of expertise and ideas between the groups of Prof. Collman, Prof. [[Henry Taube]], and Prof. [[Eugene van Tamelen]] at Stanford, and this stimulating atmosphere played a major role in the development of Prof. Gladysz's future research on the organic/inorganic interface.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Book Review: Principles and Applications of Organotransition Metal Chemistry |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/anie.198809841  |year=1988 |volume=27 |issue=7 |pages=984–985 |doi=10.1002/anie.198809841 |access-date=5 November 2020|last1=Werner |first1=Helmut |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

== Professional career ==
When Gladysz began as an assistant professor at UCLA on July 1, 1974, he was, at least for the next six weeks, 21 years of age. This early start, coupled with the active program of seminar visitors at UCLA, allowed him to get to know many organic and inorganic chemists who began their careers shortly after the Second World War. Although he developed interests in metal atom chemistry and hydride reagents for organic synthesis, he made his early reputation in C<sub>1</sub> chemistry – specifically the chemistry of metal formyl (-CHO), hydroxymethyl (-CH<sub>2</sub>OH), [[formaldehyde]] (H<sub>2</sub>C=O), and methylidene (=CH<sub>2</sub>) complexes, as well as related species that were rare at that time (and believed to be intermediates in catalytic CO/H<sub>2</sub> chemistry).<ref>{{cite journal |title=Electrophile-induced disproportionation of the neutral formyl |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/ja00512a069 |journal=Journal of the American Chemical Society |date=August 1979 |volume=101 |issue=18 |pages=5440–5442 |doi=10.1021/ja00512a069 |access-date=2 November 2020|last1=Wong |first1=Wai-Kwok |last2=Tam |first2=Wilson |last3=Gladysz |first3=J. A. |url-access=subscription }}</ref>

While at UCLA, Gladysz was named a fellow of the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation (1980)<ref>{{cite web |title=Past Fellows |url=https://sloan.org/past-fellows |website=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation |access-date=5 November 2020 |archive-date=14 March 2018 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180314000756/https://sloan.org/past-fellows }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |title=Alfred P. Sloan Foundation |url=https://sloan.org/past-fellows?mobileformat=false&page=416 |website=sloan.org |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> and a recipient of Camille and Henry Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Grant (1980).<ref>{{cite web |title=Camille Dreyfus Teacher-Scholar Awards Program |url=https://www.dreyfus.org/camille-dreyfus-teacher-scholar/ |website=Dreyfus.org |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref> In July 1982, he relocated to the University of Utah, where his research expanded to include organometallic stereochemistry and applications in enantioselective organic synthesis. While there, he received an Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award (1988),<ref>{{cite web |title=Arthur C. Cope Scholar Awards |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/arthur-cope-scholar-award.html |website=ACS Chemistry for Life |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> the University of Utah Distinguished Research Award (1992),<ref>{{cite web |title=Distinguished Scholarly & Creative Research Award Recipients |url=https://research.utah.edu/funding/recipients/dra.php |website=The University of UTAH |access-date=21 October 2020 |archive-date=31 October 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201031230434/https://research.utah.edu/funding/recipients/dra.php }}</ref> and a Humboldt Foundation Research Award for Senior Scientists (1995-1996).<ref>{{cite web |title=Humboldt Foundation Recipient |url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2010/june/gladysz-is-new-editor-in-chief-of-american-chemical-societys-organometallics.html |website=ACS.org |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref> In conjunction with the latter, he spent six months at the [[University of Marburg]], and then a final month at the [[Technical University of Munich]].

In the course of the Humboldt sponsored sabbatical, Prof. Gladysz gave a seminar at the [[ETH Zurich]]. His hosts invited the seminar speaker scheduled for the next day, Prof. Janet Bluemel (Technical University of Munich), to the customary dinner (''Nachsitzung''). This introduction led to a variety of interactions during his subsequent stay in Munich. These in turn led to their marriage on December 28, 1997, in Salt Lake City.<ref>{{cite web |title=Marriage Certificate |url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/rgroup/gladysz/documents/mcertificate.PDF |website=Gladysz Group TAMU |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref> Prof. Gladysz subsequently assumed the Chair of Organic Chemistry at the University of Erlangen-Nuremberg, where he succeeded [[Paul von Ragué Schleyer|Paul von Rague Schleyer]], on April 1, 1998; Prof. Bluemel assumed a professorship on the same day at the University of Heidelberg.<ref>{{cite web |title=Project D1 |url=https://www.uni-heidelberg.de/institute/fak12/OC/hofmann/sfb623/d/d1_e.html |website=uni-heidelberg.de |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref>

During his period in Germany, Gladysz was able to greatly expand his programs dealing with molecular wires and fluorous chemistry begun at Utah. [[István T. Horváth]], then working at ExxonMobil's Corporate Research Laboratories was a frequent collaborator on the latter project. Prof. Gladysz established a number of novel ring-closing metatheses in metal coordination spheres, the most interesting of which afforded a class of compounds that can be regarded as "molecular gyroscopes". Prof. Gladysz enjoyed all levels of the German and European scientific scenes and received the [[International Fluorous Technologies]] Award in 2007. However, he and Prof. Bluemel sought to optimize their personal and professional lives with appointments at the same University.<ref>{{cite web |title=Research Active Faculty |url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/faculty/ |website=Texas A&M University |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref>

This goal was realized during 2007-2008 when Bluemel and Gladysz relocated to Texas A&M University. Prof. Gladysz was appointed as the Dow Chair in Chemical Invention and Distinguished Professor of Chemistry.<ref>{{cite web |title=Faculty Web Page |url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/faculty/john-gladysz/ |website=Texas A&M University |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref> He was furthermore elected as a Fellow of the American Chemical Society in the inaugural year, 2009,<ref>{{cite web |title=Five Texas A&M Chemists Named to Inaugural Class of ACS Fellows |url=https://science.tamu.edu/news/2009/07/five-texas-am-chemists-named-to-inaugural-class-of-acs-fellows/ |website=science.tamu.edu |date=29 July 2009 |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> and a Fellow of the Royal Society of Chemistry in 2013.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Royal Society of Chemistry Awards 2013 |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/full/10.1002/anie.201305988 |journal=Angewandte Chemie International Edition |year=2013 |volume=52 |issue=41 |pages=10690–10691 |doi=10.1002/anie.201305988 |bibcode=2013ACIE...5210690. |access-date=21 October 2020|url-access=subscription }}</ref> Prof. Gladysz' research at Texas A&M has continued to prominently feature catalysis (phase transfer catalyst activation;<ref>{{cite journal |title=Phase Transfer Activation of Fluorous Analogs of Grubbs' Second-Generation Catalyst: Ring-Opening Metathesis Polymerization |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/10.1021/cs200487j |journal=ACS Catalysis |year=2012 |doi=10.1021/cs200487j |access-date=5 November 2020|last1=Tuba |first1=Robert |last2=Corrêa Da Costa |first2=Rosenildo |last3=Bazzi |first3=Hassan S. |last4=Gladysz |first4=John A. |volume=2 |pages=155–162 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> Werner complexes as chiral hydrogen bond donor catalysts),<ref>{{cite journal |title=Launching Werner Complexes into the Modern Era of Catalytic Enantioselective Organic Synthesis |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/acs.accounts.0c00410 |journal=Accounts of Chemical Research |year=2020 |doi=10.1021/acs.accounts.0c00410 |access-date=5 November 2020|last1=Wegener |first1=Aaron R. |last2=Kabes |first2=Connor Q. |last3=Gladysz |first3=John A. |volume=53 |issue=10 |pages=2299–2313 |pmid=32886471 |s2cid=221502289 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> and expanded into container molecules that "turn themselves inside out".<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zarcone |first1=S. R. |last2=Bhuvanesh |first2=N. |last3=Gladysz |first3=J. A. |year=2023 |title=Molecules that Turn Themselves Inside-Out: Tuning in/out Equilibria and Homeomorphic Isomerization in Macrobicyclic Dibridgehead Diphosphines P((CH2)n)3P Newly Accessible by Earth-Abundant-Metal Templates |url=https://chemistry-europe.onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/epdf/10.1002/chem.202302200 |journal=Chemistry: A European Journal |volume=29 |issue=72 |article-number=e202302200 |doi=10.1002/chem.202302200 |pmid= 37738010|doi-access=free|url-access=subscription }}</ref> He received the Texas A&M Distinguished Achievement Award in Research,<ref>{{cite web |title=Recipients of The Association of Former Students Distinguished Achievement Awards University Level |url=https://dof.tamu.edu/dof/media/PITO-DOF/AFS%20DAA/AFS-DAA-University-Level-All-Winners_1.pdf |website=Texas A&M DOF |access-date=5 November 2020 |archive-date=17 May 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210517064611/https://dof.tamu.edu/dof/media/PITO-DOF/AFS%20DAA/AFS-DAA-University-Level-All-Winners_1.pdf }}</ref> and the Royal Society of Chemistry Award in Organometallic Chemistry,<ref>{{cite web |title=Organometallic Award Winner 2013 |url=https://www.rsc.org/ScienceAndTechnology/Awards/OrganometallicChemistryAward/2013-Winner.asp |website=RSC |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref> both in 2013.

In 2017, Prof. Gladysz and Prof. Bluemel were jointly awarded the Texas A&M Foundation Partners in Philanthropy Faculty Award.<ref>{{cite web |title=PARTNER IN PHILANTHROPY AWARD |url=https://www.txamfoundation.com/News/Partner-in-Philanthropy-Award.aspx |website=Texas A&M Foundation |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref> They live on the Crow's Nest Ranch,<ref>{{Cite web|last=|first=|date=|title=Ranch Map|url=https://www.chem.tamu.edu/rgroup/gladysz/documents/maptoranch.pdf|website=}}</ref> which consists of 140 acres (60 hectares) 4 miles east of College Station.

== Research interests ==
Gladysz research centers around organometallic chemistry, and from this core branches into nanotechnology, stereochemistry, organic synthesis, enantioselective reactions, catalysis, mechanism, and materials chemistry.  This work has been described in nearly 500 widely cited publications.<ref>{{cite web |title=ORCID Reference Page |url=https://orcid.org/0000-0002-7012-4872 |website=John A. Gladysz |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref>

== Professional services and consulting ==
From June 1984 through July 2010, he was an associate editor of ''Chemical Reviews<ref>{{cite web |title=New Editor For Organometallics |url=https://cen.acs.org/articles/88/i18/New-Editor-Organometallics.html |website=C&EN |access-date=5 November 2020}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1021/cen-v088n018.p009a|title=PUBLISHING Texas A&M's John Gladysz succeeds founding editor|year=2010|last1=Rovner|first1=Sophie|journal=Chemical & Engineering News|volume=88|issue=18|page=9}}</ref>'', where he and Editor-in-Chief Prof. Josef Michl introduced a number of innovative new features. He then succeeded Prof. Dietmar Seyferth as the editor in chief of ''Organometallics'',<ref>{{cite journal |title=PUBLISHING Texas A&M's John Gladysz succeeds founding editor |url=https://pubs.acs.org/doi/abs/10.1021/cen-v088n018.p009a |journal=Chemical & Engineering News |year=2010 |doi=10.1021/cen-v088n018.p009a |access-date=5 November 2020|last1=Rovner |first1=Sophie |volume=88 |issue=18 |page=9 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> a position he held until January 2015. As an author, Prof. Gladysz has published nearly 500 journal articles and book chapters with over 23,500 independent citations and an h-index of 80.<ref>{{cite web |title=John A. Gladysz |url=https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=VO44OC0AAAAJ&hl=en |website=Google Scholar |access-date=21 October 2020}}</ref> These are augmented by nearly 100 Editorials, patents and patent applications, and book and meeting reviews.
